title: Position verification that works in physical spacetime

concept.text: The innovation would let verifiers establish that a responding party is physically present in a specified region, despite colluding attackers outside that region trying to impersonate someone inside it. An interactive protocol would make the timing and handling of challenges depend on physical location. The intended security would cover attackers who coordinate their responses and share quantum entanglement, under an explicitly stated adversary model. The supplied source establishes position verification as the underlying cryptographic goal; it does not establish that this realistic physical capability has been achieved.

Conceptual scope: the credential being tested is presence at a place. A successful protocol would authenticate a claimed location; it would not by itself identify the person or device there. The intended version would make location useful without relying on a pre-shared identity secret, but the retained abstract does not specify enough of the setup to establish that property for its reported protocols. Turning verified presence into a positioning service or a message that can be decrypted only at that location would require additional constructions.

significance.text: If realized under realistic physical assumptions, relay-resistant location authentication would make physical presence a substantial cryptographic resource. A verifier could condition an interaction on evidence that a responder occupies a room or site, even when remote parties cooperate to forge that evidence. The supplied abstract states that classical position verification is impossible in its position-verification setting. A physically implementable quantum solution against the stated entangled attackers would therefore overcome a fundamental obstacle within that setting, rather than merely improve ordinary location measurement.

Conditional downstream possibilities: a separate encryption construction might use position verification to control access to a message at a specified site. That would require a security argument connecting successful location verification to access to the plaintext; the reported position-verification result alone does not supply it. Broader positioning services and quantum-network applications would also need communications infrastructure, operational protocols, and deployment engineering. These are possible uses of the capability, not demonstrated consequences of the supplied work.

Limits on the impact: authenticating location would not automatically establish identity, trustworthiness, or authorization. Nor does the abstract's classical impossibility statement establish impossibility for every system called location authentication under different trust assumptions. The revolutionary claim is conditional on obtaining a useful physical protocol with a clearly specified security model; an idealized timing theorem alone does not deliver that operational capability.

missing_breakthrough.text: The target capability is a position-verification protocol whose security argument survives realistic implementation: clocks have finite resolution, challenge times must be generated and represented physically, responses take time to compute, and signals propagate through actual channels. Behera and Goyal's reported continuous-time advance uses real-valued time and challenge messages sent at times sampled uniformly from a real interval. Establishing what security survives physically realizable timing is therefore a central bridge to the proposed innovation. The retained abstract does not establish that computation is assumed instantaneous, and it does not justify treating finite signal speed as absent from the authors' model.

The attacker model is equally important. The continuous-time result is reported for any finite coalition of adversaries restricted to local operations and classical communication, with arbitrary finite quantum storage and shared entanglement. Here, local operations and classical communication means attackers act on their local quantum systems and coordinate through classical messages. These qualifications must remain attached to the theorem: the abstract does not establish security against every conceivable entangled attack. For the discrete-time protocol, the reported achievement is any desired polynomial gap between honest-party resources and the adversarial resource bound. Translating that gap into practical parameters requires information unavailable in the retained abstract.

Engineering synthesis: a convincing implementation would need to account for timing uncertainty, channel and processing delays, loss and noise, verifier geometry, and attackers positioned close to the accepted region's boundary. It would need to explain how those effects alter honest acceptance and attacker success, and how physical resource limits correspond to the mathematical adversary model. These are requirements for bridging the reported theory to the proposed experiment, not documented failures of the paper. The supplied evidence cannot determine which have already been addressed elsewhere.

current_state.text: Amit Behera and Vipul Goyal's “Breaking the Bounded Entanglement Barrier for Quantum Position Verification,” IACR ePrint 2026/2301, was received on 1 October 2026 and approved by the archive on 4 October 2026. It is a reported theoretical advance in an ePrint preprint. The supplied review retained the abstract and metadata page, not the full paper or proofs; archive approval does not establish peer-review validation.

The abstract records two obstacles as prior work: classical position verification is impossible in the setting under discussion, and quantum position verification admits an attack using local operations and classical communication when the adversary holds an exponentially large amount of pre-shared entanglement. The later continuous-time result changes the model, so the prior attack statement and the new security statement should not be treated as an unexplained contradiction. Their exact relationship depends on model details beyond the retained abstract.

In the continuous-time model, the abstract reports a BB84-based protocol secure against any finite coalition of adversaries using local operations and classical communication, with arbitrary finite, potentially exponential, quantum storage and entanglement. Time is represented by a real-valued parameter, and challenge messages may be sent at times sampled uniformly from a real interval. This is a reported security theorem under an idealized timing model, not an experimental demonstration. The available material does not establish computation latency assumptions or whose entanglement requirements would be excluded by the earlier phrase “no shared entanglement.”

For discrete time, the abstract reports a protocol with any desired polynomial gap between honest-party resources and the adversarial resource bound. That is a resource-separation result, not the same claim as continuous-time security with arbitrary finite entanglement. The retained page does not provide the proofs, parameter choices, or implementation requirements needed to assess concrete costs or experimental feasibility.

The retained abstract and metadata page provides no laboratory demonstration against entangled colluders. The supplied review also has no bounded search record or freshness evidence establishing whether a small optical experiment or room-scale demonstration existed elsewhere by 1 November 2026. Consequently, the record supports the dated theoretical reports but cannot establish the contemporary experimental frontier. This access limitation neither disproves an experiment elsewhere nor invalidates the reported theoretical results.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed experimental target: demonstrate that verifiers accept an honest prover inside a specified region of diameter at most 10 meters while accepting colluding exterior attackers with probability at most 2^−20 per explicitly defined trial. These numerical bounds are proposed evaluation targets, not documented achievements or established standards. Before testing, specify an honest acceptance threshold, the verifier arrangement, the region's boundary and any exclusion margin, and the attackers' allowed operations, communications, quantum storage, and shared entanglement.
completion_criteria.label: Honest acceptance within ≤10-meter-diameter regions; exterior-attacker success ≤2^−20 per trial

completion_criteria.text: Proposed physical validation: make signal travel time the operative constraint and publish a timing budget covering clock resolution, synchronization uncertainty, challenge generation, processing, and channel delays. State how loss, noise, calibration error, and boundary proximity affect acceptance. The security analysis should explain which idealizations remain and why the implemented protocol meets its stated adversary model. An idealized timing theorem alone would not meet this laboratory target.
completion_criteria.label: Signal travel time constrains responses under published physical timing budgets

completion_criteria.text: Proposed evidentiary standard: combine an implementation-specific security argument with reproducible experiments, independent replication, and documented attacks within the declared model. Report trial definitions, parameter choices, measured honest acceptance, attacker success, uncertainty, and the basis for any claimed 2^−20 bound. A finite attack campaign demonstrates tested breadth; it cannot by itself prove security against every allowed strategy or literally test arbitrary finite entanglement. Any general attacker bound must come from an applicable security argument whose physical assumptions are justified.
completion_criteria.label: Implementation-specific security supported by reproducible experiments and independent replication

completion_criteria.text: Proposed application extension: separately construct and demonstrate location-bound decryption, specifying how verification controls access to plaintext and what security is claimed against remote colluders. This would show an additional cryptographic use of verified presence. It should be assessed independently from the core position-verification demonstration, with practical boundaries stated rather than inferred from the location test.
completion_criteria.label: Location-bound decryption controls plaintext access with stated remote-collusion security

related_concepts.text: Roster comparison—CRY-01, “A proof that an explicit one-way function exists,” and CRY-02, “Public-key encryption from one-way functions”: all concern foundations of cryptographic capability. CRY-01 asks for an explicit computational hardness foundation, and CRY-02 asks whether a particular assumption can support public-key encryption. CRY-07 instead asks whether physical location can be verified against coordinated attackers. Neither roster entry by itself supplies position verification, and CRY-07 would not resolve either foundational question.

Roster comparison—CRY-03, “Practically efficient post-quantum indistinguishability obfuscation,” CRY-04, “General-purpose private computation at near-plaintext cost,” and CRY-08, “Metadata-private messaging at ordinary cost”: these concern hiding program information, computing privately, or concealing communication metadata. CRY-07 concerns establishing presence at a place. Such capabilities might be composed in future systems, but location verification alone supplies none of those privacy or efficiency guarantees. In particular, verifying a location is distinct from protecting location-related metadata.

Roster comparison—CRY-05, “Publicly verifiable unclonable money and copy-protected programs,” and CRY-06, “Practical classical verification of quantum computation”: these overlap with CRY-07 in seeking cryptographic capabilities connected to quantum systems. Their verification targets differ: CRY-05 concerns authenticity or controlled copying, CRY-06 concerns correctness of quantum computation, and CRY-07 concerns physical presence. Security or practical progress on one target does not establish the others.

Roster comparison—CRY-09, “Post-quantum timed release with a sequentiality theorem,” and CRY-10, “A conclusive quantum classification of deployed lattice encryption”: CRY-09 shares an interest in time as a security constraint, but delaying access through sequential computation differs from verifying location through physical timing and signal propagation. CRY-10 concerns the quantum security classification of deployed encryption, whereas CRY-07 concerns colluding attackers in a spatial protocol. A position-verification result does not classify lattice encryption, and a sequentiality theorem does not by itself establish presence at a location. These comparisons are conceptual synthesis from the supplied roster titles.

brief.title: Proof that someone is really at a place
possible: A service could check that a responder is inside a particular room or site, even when people elsewhere cooperate to fake that presence. Physical location would become something the responder could prove through an exchange of signals.
why: Systems could make access depend on physical presence despite coordinated remote impersonation. This would give people protecting sensitive sites a way to carry some of the security of being there into digital interactions.

sources.showed: Their preprint proves security with idealized continuous timing against any finite group sharing finite quantum resources, including entanglement: correlations between quantum systems. Attackers must act locally and coordinate through ordinary messages.
sources.quote: In fact, we can achieve any desired polynomial gap between honest parties and adversarial resources.
sources.cited_for: The theory extends protection against collaborating attackers with shared quantum resources.
sources.not_established: The result does not establish that its timing assumptions can survive a physical implementation.

sources.showed: They built a location-verification system combining quantum light signals with limits imposed by signal travel time. Dedicated communication links and fast processing reduced delays.
sources.quote: Here we propose and experimentally realize a secure position verification protocol that combines quantum optics and relativity within an information-theoretic framework.
sources.cited_for: A physical experiment demonstrates location verification with measured timing constraints.
sources.not_established: The experiment does not establish the target room-sized accuracy and protection against the full intended range of attackers.

sources.showed: Their preprint reports an experiment that verifies location without trusting the quantum devices’ internal workings. Its demonstrated security allows only very weak prior entanglement between attackers.
sources.quote:
We
experimentally implement a version of this device-independent protocol against
adversaries who, before each trial, are weakly entangled.
sources.cited_for: Location verification can work experimentally with fewer trust assumptions about quantum hardware.
sources.not_established: The implemented version does not establish protection against attackers sharing arbitrary finite entanglement.

sources.who: Llorenç Escolà-Farràs, Boris Škorić and Florian Speelman
sources.showed: Their preprint proves that a single location check can tolerate arbitrarily large transmission loss while bounding attackers’ shared entanglement. It also allows slow quantum communication and limited noise.
sources.quote:
As in the
underlying protocol, quantum communication need not occur at the speed of light.
sources.cited_for: Transmission loss need not prevent verification under a bounded-entanglement attacker model.
sources.not_established: This is a theoretical result under resource limits, rather than a demonstration meeting the physical target.

sources.showed: They proved that sufficiently large shared entanglement defeats position verification in their model. They also constructed secure schemes when attackers share no entanglement, including ways to establish secret communication.
sources.quote:
As a consequence, we show a generic
attack that breaks any position-veriﬁcation scheme.
sources.cited_for: The attacker assumptions determine whether secure verification and further location-based security are possible.
sources.not_established: The constructions do not demonstrate physical security against entangled collaborators under realistic timing.

shown: Guan-Jie Fan-Yuan and colleagues demonstrated location verification accurate to better than 75 metres. Gautam Kavuri and colleagues separately demonstrated a smaller accepted region than a comparable classical method could achieve. These experiments establish physical progress under restricted attacker assumptions.
missing: A room-sized demonstration must meet the proposed attacker-success bound with a defined honest acceptance threshold.
A physical security argument must account for clock uncertainty, processing delays, signal loss, noise and attackers near the boundary.
The target implementation still needs independent replication and a separate demonstration of messages accessible only at the verified location.

milestones.label: Room-sized verification with bounded attacker success
milestones.explanation: A test would have to accept an honest responder within a region at most 10 metres across while meeting the proposed exterior-attacker success bound. This would establish the target accuracy and resistance to impersonation.

milestones.label: Signal travel time governs responses under measured delays
milestones.explanation: An experiment would have to show that signal travel time constrains responses, with a published account of timing uncertainty and delays. This would connect the security argument to physical equipment.

milestones.label: Reproducible security with independent replication
milestones.explanation: An implementation would need a justified security argument, reproducible experiments, independent replication and documented attacks within its stated model. Together, these would support protection beyond the attacks directly tested.

milestones.label: Messages unlocked only at the verified location
milestones.explanation: A separate construction would have to restrict access to a message’s contents to the verified location, with stated protection against remote collaborators. This would turn verified presence into control over message access.

uncertain: How much security survives when perfectly precise mathematical timing becomes physically generated and measured timing?
How does the continuous-time result relate to earlier attacks under different timing assumptions?
What trial definition, boundary margin and attacker limits would justify the proposed success bound?

page.title: Quantum position verification with a resource gap
page.definition: Trusted verifiers would use quantum challenges and timed responses to establish that a device acted inside a specified region, without sharing an identity secret with the device. At the experiment’s timing resolution, the security proof would cover colluding outsiders whose combined quantum memory can exceed all the classical bits and qubits the prover and verifiers communicate or store. The outsiders may perform local quantum operations and exchange classical messages.

goal.need: In Ontario’s first year of regulated online gaming, one provider recorded over 3.3 million attempts to fake a user’s location. More precise classical ranging still lets colluding outsiders return the right answer on time. A bank could make presence at a branch a condition for accepting a transaction, even when outsiders control more quantum memory than the branch and its verifiers use for all communication and storage. The bank would still need a separate credential to identify the customer.

completion.title: A finite-clock position-verification experiment retains a proved honest–attacker resource gap.
completion.criterion: Demonstrate a finite-clock protocol family with total honest communication and storage ≤t and negligible acceptance probability for every finite, fixed-position coalition outside the accepted region holding ≤r qubits, with r>t. Colluders may perform local quantum operations and communicate classically. At the tested settings, report numerical t and r with r>t, the accepted region, and honest-acceptance and soundness bounds that account for measured timing uncertainty, processing delay, loss and noise. The honest device must pass the specified test.
completion.set_by: Technology Atlas synthesis of the implementation goal and the published t-versus-r resource-gap definition; no common physical completion standard was found.
completion.basis: The Atlas combines a physical demonstration with Behera and Goyal’s t-versus-r security definition. Their definition supplies the resource comparison. The physical pass rule has no common certification standard. In discrete time the gap depends on the challenge slots the entire apparatus can distinguish. The continuous-time theorem assumes timing precision unavailable to a physical system.

milestones.title: A Bell-test location check passes at 2⁻⁶⁴ soundness against colluders without prior entanglement.
milestones.criterion: For a basic Bell-test instance, determine the target spacetime region from the verifier geometry and timing windows. Multiply the calibrated test factors over 30 million trials. Accept if the product reaches 2⁶⁴. The false-acceptance probability is at most 2⁻⁶⁴ for outsiders with no shared entanglement before each trial. The calibration target for honest acceptance is 0.97725.
milestones.set_by: Kavuri and colleagues, basic Bell-test protocol and experimental analysis.
milestones.threshold_quote: A product $P\geq 2^{64}$ results in a pass

milestones.title: A Bell-test location check passes with mean adversarial entanglement robustness bounded by 8×10⁻⁶.
milestones.criterion: For an extended Bell-test instance, multiply the entanglement-adjusted test factors over 60 million trials and accept if the product reaches 2⁶⁴. The false-acceptance probability is at most 2⁻⁶⁴ when the robustness of the outsiders’ shared state before each trial averages at most 8×10⁻⁶ over the instance. A Bell pair has robustness 1.
milestones.set_by: Kavuri and colleagues, extended Bell-test protocol and experimental analysis.
milestones.threshold_quote: the robustness threshold was fixed at $r_{\text{th}}=8\times 10^{-6}$.

milestones.title: A single loss-tolerant execution is secure for every fixed error fraction below (1−1/√2)/2.
milestones.criterion: Set γ*=(1−1/√2)/2. For 0≤γ<γ*, prove attacker acceptance ≤3·2^(−kD₂(γ‖γ*)), where D₂ is binary relative entropy in bits. Require 1≤k≤m<n and 4q≤n−k/4−log₂n−7. Of m transmitted qubits, at least k must be declared received before the n-bit classical inputs arrive. Both verifiers must receive the same timely answer, with error fraction ≤γ on committed positions. Each attacker holds at most q qubits before intercepting the classical inputs. The bound must hold for at least 1−2⁻ⁿ of uniformly sampled protocol functions and permit arbitrary transmission loss and arbitrarily slow quantum communication.
milestones.set_by: Escolà-Farràs, Škorić and Speelman, Theorem 5.7, with the committed-subset bound of Escolà-Farràs and Speelman, section 5.

milestones.title: A discrete-time protocol family attains each prescribed polynomial resource gap.
milestones.criterion: For each prescribed polynomial gap, choose polynomially bounded parameters m, s and R, with m/log₂²λ→∞, s≥9 slots per round and R≥1 stored prover qubits. For two static verifiers in one dimension, prove total honest communication and storage Õ(R+m). Every finite coalition at fixed exterior positions that succeeds with non-negligible probability must hold Ω(smR/log₂²λ) qubits in total. Colluders use local quantum operations and classical communication with unrestricted classical resources. The model assumes perfect quantum communication and instantaneous local operations.
milestones.set_by: Behera and Goyal, discrete-time protocol, Theorems 2 and 7; one-dimensional static verifiers.
milestones.threshold_quote: for every polynomial $p(\lambda)$ there is a protocol in the family that achieves that resource gap $p(\lambda)$.

milestones.title: A two-photon prover beats the 2/3 bound for correct answers on conclusive trials.
milestones.criterion: Prepare equally likely parallel and orthogonal photon polarizations in the protocol’s three mutually unbiased bases. Interfere each pair at a beam splitter and classify conclusive two-detector coincidences. The mean probability of correctly distinguishing parallel from orthogonal inputs, conditioned on a conclusive result, must exceed 2/3, the bound for two outsiders using local operations and classical communication without shared entanglement.
milestones.set_by: Kanneworff and colleagues, four-detector position-verification protocol, equation 2 and figure 4.
milestones.threshold_quote: The ‘LOCC limit’ of 2/3 is the maximal achievable probability for attackers

milestones.title: A coherent-state location check scores at least −242,972 in 10 million rounds.
milestones.criterion: Use phase-randomized optical pulses with mean photon number 0.52 and a 40-bit classical challenge. Over 10⁷ rounds, score each correct response +0.04275, each incorrect or discarded response −1, and each no-response event −0.05019. Require a total score ≥−242,972. Bound the possible location by intersecting the two verifier-centred regions whose radii are half the respective round-trip times multiplied by the speed of light in vacuum.
milestones.set_by: Fan-Yuan and colleagues, coherent-state position-verification protocol, position inference and finite-size score.
milestones.threshold_quote: In this case, $\Gamma_{0}$ is calculated as $-242972$.

milestones.title: The apparatus resolves at least nine challenge slots in one protocol time unit.
milestones.criterion: For the one-dimensional discrete-time protocol, demonstrate s≥9 reliably distinguishable challenge times within the unit interval used in the security bound. Determine s for the synchronized control, transmission and detection system, allowing for the prover’s processing delay when setting the slot spacing and response deadline.
milestones.set_by: Behera and Goyal, timing hypothesis of Theorem 3, implementation qualification in footnote 2 and discussion of non-instantaneous computation.
milestones.threshold_quote: s\geq 9,R_{H}\geq 1$ be integer protocol parameters. Suppose there is a clock with $s$ reliably distinguishable ticks in a unit interval of time.

not_found: No common physical quantum-position-verification certification test or fixed localization and error thresholds were found in the standards and roadmap searches.
No physical demonstration of the Behera–Goyal finite-clock resource-gap protocol was found.
No experiment was found that establishes a numerical attacker-storage bound above total honest communication and storage at its measured operating parameters.
No standards body, roadmap committee or funding programme was found that judges a physical bounded-resource gap unattainable or unworthy of pursuit.

definition = "Trusted verifiers would use quantum challenges and timed responses to establish that a device acted inside a specified region, without sharing an identity secret with the device. At the experiment\u2019s timing resolution, the security proof would cover colluding outsiders whose combined quantum memory can exceed all the classical bits and qubits the prover and verifiers communicate or store. The outsiders may perform local quantum operations and exchange classical messages.". Reason: The definition leaves unclear what timing establishes, which resources the comparison counts and how the colluders may communicate.

goal.need = "In Ontario\u2019s first year of regulated online gaming, one provider recorded over 3.3 million attempts to fake a user\u2019s location. More precise classical ranging still lets colluding outsiders return the right answer on time. A bank could make presence at a branch a condition for accepting a transaction, even when outsiders control more quantum memory than the branch and its verifiers use for all communication and storage. The bank would still need a separate credential to identify the customer.". Reason: The current paragraph gives an experiment’s round count and refers to a missing table without explaining who needs trustworthy location evidence.

edit completion: criterion = "Demonstrate a finite-clock protocol family with total honest communication and storage \u2264t and negligible acceptance probability for every finite, fixed-position coalition outside the accepted region holding \u2264r qubits, with r>t. Colluders may perform local quantum operations and communicate classically. At the tested settings, report numerical t and r with r>t, the accepted region, and honest-acceptance and soundness bounds that account for measured timing uncertainty, processing delay, loss and noise. The honest device must pass the specified test."; set_by_kind = "atlas"; basis = "The Atlas combines a physical demonstration with Behera and Goyal\u2019s t-versus-r security definition. Their definition supplies the resource comparison. The physical pass rule has no common certification standard. In discrete time the gap depends on the challenge slots the entire apparatus can distinguish. The continuous-time theorem assumes timing precision unavailable to a physical system."; refs = [5, 8, 3, 4, 2]. Reason: The criterion requires a resource gap for the protocol family but does not explicitly require the two budgets to be evaluated at the experimental settings.

edit m1: criterion = "For a basic Bell-test instance, determine the target spacetime region from the verifier geometry and timing windows. Multiply the calibrated test factors over 30 million trials. The calibration target for honest acceptance is 0.97725."; threshold_quote = "A product $P\\geq 2^{64}$ results in a pass"; threshold_ref = 6; refs = [6, 13]. edit m2: criterion = "For an extended Bell-test instance, multiply the entanglement-adjusted test factors over 60 million trials and accept if the product reaches 2\u2076\u2074. edit m3: title = "A single loss-tolerant execution is secure for every fixed error fraction below (1\u22121/\u221a2)/2."; criterion = "Set \u03b3*=(1\u22121/\u221a2)/2. For 0\u2264\u03b3<\u03b3*, prove attacker acceptance \u22643\u00b72^(\u2212kD\u2082(\u03b3\u2016\u03b3*)), where D\u2082 is binary relative entropy in bits. Require 1\u2264k\u2264m<n and 4q\u2264n\u2212k/4\u2212log\u2082n\u22127. Of m transmitted qubits, at least k must be declared received before the n-bit classical inputs arrive. Both verifiers must receive the same timely answer, with error fraction \u2264\u03b3 on committed positions. Each attacker holds at most q qubits before intercepting the classical inputs. The bound must hold for at least 1\u22122\u207b\u207f of uniformly sampled protocol functions and permit arbitrary transmission loss and arbitrarily slow quantum communication."; set_by = "Escol\u00e0-Farr\u00e0s, \u0160kori\u0107 and Speelman, Theorem 5.7, with the committed-subset bound of Escol\u00e0-Farr\u00e0s and Speelman, section 5."; set_by_kind = "protocol"; threshold_quote = "from approximately $3.7\\%$ to every fixed $\\gamma<\\gamma_{*}\\approx 14.64\\%$."; threshold_ref = 12; refs = [7, 12]. Reason: The sharper error bound applies explicitly to the committed subset in m3 and preserves the original conditions on attacker memory and function choice.

edit m4: title = "A discrete-time protocol family attains each prescribed polynomial resource gap."; criterion = "For each prescribed polynomial gap, choose polynomially bounded parameters m, s and R, with m/log\u2082\u00b2\u03bb\u2192\u221e, s\u22659 slots per round and R\u22651 stored prover qubits. For two static verifiers in one dimension, prove total honest communication and storage \u00d5(R+m). Every finite coalition at fixed exterior positions that succeeds with non-negligible probability must hold \u03a9(smR/log\u2082\u00b2\u03bb) qubits in total. Colluders use local quantum operations and classical communication with unrestricted classical resources. The model assumes perfect quantum communication and instantaneous local operations."; threshold_quote = "for every polynomial $p(\\lambda)$ there is a protocol in the family that achieves that resource gap $p(\\lambda)$."; threshold_ref = 5; refs = [5]. Reason: The theorem allows a different family member for each prescribed polynomial gap and leaves a single protocol achieving every polynomial gap open.
